820.title: The ladder of love
820.hook: Diotima teaches Socrates that love climbs from one beautiful person to beauty itself (Symposium 210–211)
820.howItsDone: Readers of Plato's Symposium, in philosophy classes and in some mystical writing shaped by Plato, discuss Diotima's ascent from the love of one person to the love of beauty itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was chesed, loyal, steady kindness. Your line was many words. Today, one more Greek word, and a staircase.

A dinner party in Athens, in Plato's Symposium. The guests agree to go easy on the wine and take turns giving speeches in praise of love. When it's Socrates' turn, the famous talker does something odd: he doesn't offer his own view. A wise woman from Mantinea named Diotima taught him what love is, he says, and he simply passes her lesson on. It has a shape, and the shape is a climb.
screen: `A DINNER PARTY IN ATHENS.` → `SOCRATES PASSES IT ON.` → `DIOTIMA OF MANTINEA.`

segments.voice: First, one beautiful person. The Greek word all night is eros, love as longing, love that wants what it doesn't yet have. Diotima says this love often begins with one beautiful person, and the lover is moved to speak beautiful words. Second, beauty in others. The lover notices that the beauty in one body is akin to the beauty in another, and the love widens past a single face. Third, beauty of soul: the beauty of minds and character, then of good laws and ways of living, then of knowledge. Fourth, beauty itself. At the top, Diotima says, the lover suddenly sees a beauty that doesn't grow or fade, isn't lovely in one way and ugly in another, and is the source of every beautiful thing below it. Readers call it the ladder of love, because she describes going up as if by steps. Some hear it as climbing away from people. Others hear the first love as the bottom rung: not thrown away, and without it there's no ladder at all. Plato leaves room for both readings. What's plain in the text is the direction: love, for Diotima, keeps reaching past the thing it started with.

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on something beautiful near you, or bring one to mind: a face, a line of music, a kind act you once saw, an idea that made you sit up. After a few breaths, let your attention climb one step and ask what it is in this that lifts you, not the thing itself but its beauty. If nothing comes, stay on the first rung; it's part of the ladder too.
Eros. Love as longing, the force in Plato's Symposium that climbs, step by step, from one beautiful person toward beauty itself. Today's word.
Your line: the ladder. The first rung counts too, and so does the climb. See you tomorrow.

821.title: The other half
821.hook: Aristophanes' myth: humans split in two, searching for their other half (Symposium 189–193)
821.howItsDone: Aristophanes' myth from Plato's Symposium is read in philosophy and literature classes, and its picture of searching for one's other half turns up in writing about love; readers take it as comedy, as a myth, or both.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was eros, love as longing, climbing Diotima's ladder. Your line was the ladder. Today, the same dinner party, and a very different speech.

Earlier that night at the Symposium, before Socrates speaks, it's the comic playwright Aristophanes' turn, and he has the hiccups. A doctor at the table tells him to hold his breath, then to gargle with water, and if all else fails, to tickle his nose and sneeze. The doctor speaks in his place while he recovers. When Aristophanes finally gets the floor, he tells the evening's strangest story, and maybe the easiest one to remember.

First, round people. Long ago, Aristophanes says, humans were round, with four arms, four legs and two faces looking opposite ways. They ran by rolling along like tumblers turning cartwheels. There were three kinds: male, female, and a kind that was both. Second, cut in two. They grew so strong and bold that they tried to climb up and attack the gods. Zeus didn't wipe them out; he cut each one in half, and Apollo turned their faces around and drew the skin together at the navel, a mark left as a reminder. Third, the search. Ever since, each half longs for its other half. When two find each other, they don't want to be apart even for a moment, though neither can say exactly what they want. Love is the name for that desire and pursuit of the whole. Fourth, a comedy, and an answer. It's a playwright's story, told with a wink, and Plato doesn't give it the last word: later that night, Diotima says love isn't of a half or a whole unless it is good. Still, the picture has lasted. Some readers hear in it something they know: meeting a person and recognizing them.

822.title: Three friendships
822.hook: Aristotle: friendships of use, of pleasure, and of goodness (Nicomachean Ethics 8.3)
822.howItsDone: Aristotle's three kinds of friendship, from books eight and nine of the Nicomachean Ethics, are studied in philosophy and ethics courses, and some readers use them to reflect on their own friendships.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Aristophanes, and his round people cut in two. Your line was the half. Today, from a dinner party to a lecture room, and a word from earlier this week: philia.

A crowded group chat. Some people are in it because you work together, some because you have fun together. And maybe one or two are there because, if everything else fell away, you'd still want them in your life. Aristotle noticed the same sorting long before phones, in his Nicomachean Ethics, and he gave it a shape: three kinds of friendship, and a slow one at the end.

First, friends of use. Some friendships rest on what each person gets: a coworker, a neighbor who lends tools. Aristotle doesn't sneer at these, but when the usefulness ends, he says, the friendship tends to end too. Second, friends of pleasure: people who are fun, who make you laugh. He notices these among the young, who change what they enjoy, and so make and lose friends quickly. Third, friends of the good. The complete kind, Aristotle says, is between people who are good and alike in goodness, who wish good to each other for the other's own sake. These turn out pleasant and useful too, but that isn't why they exist, and they last as long as the people stay good. Fourth, salt eaten together. Such friendships are rare, he says, and slow. As the old saying goes, people can't know each other until they've eaten salt together. The wish for friendship comes fast; the friendship itself takes time. Philia is Aristotle's word for all three kinds. He doesn't call friends of use fake. He calls them a smaller kind, and keeps the larger kind for people who want each other's good.

If one name stands out, stay with it and remember the time it took, the meals and the hard days, the salt eaten together. If no name comes, that's an honest answer too, and a friendship like that can still begin.

823.title: Another self
823.hook: Aristotle: a friend is another self (Nicomachean Ethics 9.4)
823.howItsDone: Aristotle's idea of the friend as another self, from book nine of the Nicomachean Ethics, is studied in philosophy courses, and some readers use it to reflect on how they treat friends and themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was philia, Aristotle's word for the love between friends. Your line was friends of the good. Today, he goes a step further, in two Greek words.

Good news arrives, and some people's thumbs go straight to one particular name. Bad news, the same name. Nobody decided that on purpose; it just grew. In the ninth book of his Ethics, Aristotle looks at that kind of bond and asks an odd question: where does it come from? His answer starts somewhere unexpected, not with the friend at all, but with how a good person lives with themself.
screen: `ONE NAME FOR GOOD NEWS.` → `AN ODD QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the marks of a friend. Aristotle lists what people take friendship to mean: wishing good to someone for their sake, wishing them to exist and to live, spending time with them, choosing the same things, sharing their griefs and their joys. Second, it starts at home. Then he turns the list around. A good person already relates to themself this way: wants their own good, wants to go on living, is glad of their own company, and isn't at war inside. Third, another self. And so, he says, the good person is to a friend as to themself, for a friend is another self: in Greek, two words, allos autos. Not a copy. Someone whose good matters to you the way your own does, whose griefs land on you as if they were yours. Fourth, the warning inside. He then draws bad people as the opposite: at odds with themselves, running from their own company, full of regret for what they've chosen, with no friendly feeling even toward themselves. Some readers take a hopeful thought from the passage: peace inside and friendship outside may grow from the same root, and tending one may help the other.
screen: `THE MARKS OF A FRIEND.` · `IT STARTS AT HOME.` · `ALLOS AUTOS, ANOTHER SELF.` · `THE WARNING INSIDE.` · then, large: `ANOTHER SELF.`

segments.voice: Bring one friend to mind and, breathing in, wish them what you'd wish yourself today: rest, a good meal, an easy hour, some good news. Breathing out, if it isn't too hard, wish yourself the same, and go back and forth, friend and self, until the two wishes start to sound alike. If one comes easily and the other is hard, just notice which, without judging it.

824.title: Because it was he
824.hook: Montaigne on his friend La Boétie: because it was he, because it was I (Essays 1.28)
824.howItsDone: Montaigne's essay Of Friendship, from the first book of his Essays, is read in literature and philosophy courses, and some readers turn to it when they're grieving a friend.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was another self, Aristotle's allos autos. Your line was isn't at war inside. Today, his careful lists meet a friendship that wouldn't fit on any list.

Two men in France have heard about each other for a while, and each is curious about the other. Then, by chance, they meet at a great feast, in the middle of a crowd. By the end of that first meeting, one of them later wrote, they were so taken with each other that nothing was ever again as close to either of them as the other. The writer was Michel de Montaigne. The friend was Étienne de La Boétie. The essay is called, simply, Of Friendship.
screen: `A FEAST AND A CROWD.` → `MONTAIGNE AND LA BOÉTIE.`

segments.voice: First, the question he can't answer. If someone pressed him to say why he loved his friend, Montaigne says, he could only answer: because it was he, because it was I. No list of reasons, no virtues counted up. Second, the seam disappears. In this friendship, the two souls were so mingled that the seam joining them couldn't be found. He sets it apart from what he calls common friendships, where you walk with the bridle in your hand, with prudence and caution. In theirs, everything was held in common, so neither could even be said to give the other anything. Third, cut short. La Boétie died, and the friendship ended far sooner than Montaigne wanted. Set beside the time he had with his friend, he writes, the rest of his life was smoke, a long dark night. Fourth, against the list. Two days ago Aristotle explained friendship by what it rests on, and yesterday by its marks. Montaigne doesn't throw that out. But he insists a friendship like this can't be fully explained from the outside. You can describe it; you can't give its reasons. The reason is the person, two names and nothing else.
screen: `THE QUESTION HE CAN'T ANSWER.` · `THE SEAM DISAPPEARS.` · `CUT SHORT.` · `AGAINST THE LIST.` · then, large: `BECAUSE IT WAS HE.`

segments.voice: Let your deepest friendship come to mind, whether it's going on now, or faded, or lost to death, and don't explain it: just let their face, their voice, something they used to say be there. If reasons arrive, let them pass by, and rest in the plain fact of them. If no friendship like that comes, let the one you'd hope for sit there instead, without a face yet.
Montaigne, who said he loved his friend because it was he, because it was I, with no list of reasons to give. Today's word.

825.title: As yourself
825.howItsDone: Jews read Leviticus 19 in the Torah cycle as part of the portion called Kedoshim, and Hillel's answer to the man on one foot is taught in Jewish schools and sermons; Christians know the verse through Jesus' quotation of it in the Gospels.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Montaigne, who loved his friend because it was he, because it was I. Your line was smoke, a long dark night. Today, the love block turns to Jewish voices, and a line from Leviticus.

Leviticus can look like the hard book: offerings, skin diseases, rules for a plague in the walls of a house. Some readers who set out to read the Bible straight through stall right there. But chapter nineteen, in among rules about harvests and wages and fabrics, holds a line some people know by heart without knowing where it comes from. It sits in the middle of a verse, and the first half of that verse changes how it sounds.

First, the whole verse. The King James text reads: "Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." It lands right after revenge and grudges: here, loving the neighbor starts with putting a grudge down. Second, a chapter of neighbors. Around the verse are very practical laws: leave the corners of your field and the fallen grapes for the poor and the stranger; don't keep a worker's wages overnight; don't put a stumbling block before the blind. In Leviticus, love has hands. Third, the great principle. Jewish tradition records Rabbi Akiva calling this verse a great principle of the Torah. And the Talmud tells of a man who asked Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while he stood on one foot. Hillel answered: what is hateful to you, don't do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Now go and learn. Fourth, as yourself. Jesus quotes the same verse in the Gospels, a Jewish teacher quoting the Torah. And the two words at the end quietly assume something: that people want good things for themselves, and that the neighbor's wants are just as real.

826.title: You were strangers
826.hook: love the stranger, for you were strangers in Egypt (Deuteronomy 10:19)
826.howItsDone: Jewish tradition cites the Torah's command to love the stranger, remembering slavery in Egypt, in teaching about welcoming guests and newcomers, and the memory of Egypt is retold each year at the Passover seder.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was as yourself, from Leviticus nineteen. Your line was love has hands. Today, the Torah widens the circle past the neighbor, to the one who just arrived.

The first week in a new place has its own feel. Nobody tells you which door people actually use, how the bus takes payment, who to ask about the trash. You smile too much, or not enough. The Torah returns to that position more than once, the newcomer's, and asks its readers to remember standing in it. This first week of the love block ends right there, with the stranger.
screen: `A FIRST WEEK SOMEWHERE NEW.` → `THE NEWCOMER'S PLACE.`

segments.voice: First, love the stranger. In Deuteronomy, Moses describes God as the one who loves the stranger, giving him food and clothing, and then says: "Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The reason isn't an argument. It's a memory. Second, as thyself, again. Yesterday's chapter, Leviticus nineteen, says the stranger who lives with you shall be as one born among you, "and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The love owed to the neighbor is stretched, on purpose, to the outsider. Third, the heart of a stranger. Exodus puts it plainly: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." Empathy, in this text, isn't imagination. It's history carried in the body. Fourth, the week in one line. Diotima's ladder, Aristophanes' halves, Aristotle's friends, another self, Montaigne's La Boétie, Leviticus: the week began with one beautiful face and one chosen friend, and came round to the neighbor. The stranger widens the circle again: someone not chosen, not yet known, whom the Torah asks its readers to welcome anyway.

chat.says: Why does the Torah keep telling people to love the stranger?
options: Because of a memory: 'for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.'
Because strangers brought trade, so welcoming them kept the land rich.
